Comment: One cycle of the flywheel, and the loop back to the next. Every step is live: the last two stubs, Select and Purchase, now rank the pool and buy the top of it, which is what closes the loop. Start it with {"run_id": <id>, "epochs": <n>, "seeds": [1]}, and optionally max_images, replace and instance_type -- the last three apply to training and scoring alike, since both are capped and re-prepared together. A short run capped with max_images must be registered with a label budget it can afford: selection refuses a budget larger than the pool it ranked, so a 300-image cycle against the design's 1,000 is refused rather than quietly buying fewer.

ClaimCycle.Comment: The single-flight lock, and the only place a cycle number comes from. One conditional update adds one to next_cycle and returns the item as it was, so the number handed back is the cycle this execution now owns and no other execution can own. The condition carries the cap too, which is why a run that has spent its cycles is refused here rather than by a check upstream that has to remember to run. ALL_OLD rather than UPDATED_OLD because the cap and the champion are read off the same call -- the pointer `Promote` wrote at the end of the previous cycle arrives with the cycle number, so nothing reads this item twice. The champion is a ternary rather than a bare path because a run's first cycle has no such attribute, and a JSONata expression resolving to nothing fails the state; `null` is what the evaluation step reads as "this model is the run's baseline". The retries below are throttles and transient faults only: a failed condition means the cap is spent or another execution holds this run, and both are the same answer on a second attempt.

Prepare.Comment: Writes the two objects a cycle hands its seeds: the image manifest naming the cumulative labeled set, and the source archive the container unpacks. Once per cycle rather than once per seed, because the seeds of a challenger must differ in the seed and in nothing else. The retries are runtime faults and not refusals -- ControlError is what the handler raises when the work itself is refused, and it is refused identically on a second attempt. The payload is one JSONata object rather than a field per key, and that is what makes `max_images` and `replace` optional: a field whose expression resolves to nothing fails the state, while a key of an object constructor whose value resolves to nothing is simply absent -- so an execution that omits one gets the handler's default rather than States.QueryEvaluationError.

Train.Comment: One training job per seed over the cycle prepared above. The seed list is an execution input rather than a constant: the design trains one, and a run that wants the seed spread asks for more without editing the state machine. MaxConcurrency matches the design rather than the list, because the on-demand quota for the instance type is what a wider fan-out would run into -- raise both together or the extra jobs fail on ResourceLimitExceeded and burn their retries.

TrainingRequest.Comment: The request is built by the same function the CLI calls, so this file is a second caller of one definition rather than a second definition of a training job written in a language with no tests. One object for `Prepare`'s reason, and here it is what keeps the compute defaults in one place: `instance_type` is `job.Compute`'s, which the CLI reaches without passing through this file at all, so a default restated here would be a second copy of the compute policy rather than the policy.

TrainSeed.Comment: `.sync` owns the wait, so nothing in this project polls a training job or stays alive beside one, and an aborted execution stops the job rather than leaving a GPU running. There is no CheckpointConfig to resume from, so a job that runs again runs from the beginning, which is what keeps `seed k fixes the run` true. What is retried is only the failure to get an instance -- see the retrier -- and two attempts rather than many, because a job that cannot get one twice is a quota problem and not a flake.

Retry.Comment: Only what fails before a job exists. The request is built once by the step above, job name included, so a retry submits the same name -- and SageMaker refuses a duplicate with ResourceInUse. That is not a second attempt at anything: it replaces the real failure with a name clash, which is how an int8 crash was reported as ResourceInUseException. A job that was created and then failed is a cycle to look at, not to run again.

ScorePrepare.Comment: Writes the two manifests naming what this cycle scores: the frozen eval cohort, and the pool minus everything the run has bought. Once per cycle rather than once per seed, for `Prepare`'s reason -- every seed scores the same images, and two documents differing by seed would be one list written twice with nothing to say which was ranked. Placed after `Train` rather than beside `Prepare` because the pool it names is the pool this cycle's challenger will rank, and reading it later is what makes the document the record of that. The payload is one JSONata object for `Prepare`'s reason, so `max_images` and `replace` stay optional.

Score.Comment: One scoring job per seed the cycle trained, over the two manifests above. `Items` is `$seeds_trained` rather than the execution's seed list, so a seed that failed to train is a seed nothing tries to score -- and the version and seed each job needs are already in what `Train` assigned. MaxConcurrency for `Train`'s reason: these are the same GPU instance type and the same on-demand quota, so a wider fan-out here competes with nothing today and fails on ResourceLimitExceeded the moment the seed list grows.

ScoringRequest.Comment: `TrainingRequest`'s arrangement for the other job: the request is built by the same function a CLI calls, so this file is a second caller of one definition rather than a second definition written in a language with no tests. `instance_type` is the only compute field an execution may set, and the scoring recipe -- resolution, confidence floor, detection cap -- is not among them: each is pinned to a value another component depends on, so an input for one would be a way to score two cycles of one run differently.

ScoreSeed.Comment: `.sync` owns the wait, for `TrainSeed`'s reasons. A failed job restarts from the beginning, which costs a pass over the images rather than a training run and is safe to repeat: the job reads a frozen model and two frozen manifests and writes one object per cohort, so a second attempt produces the same detections and overwrites its own partial output. Two attempts rather than many -- a job that cannot get an instance twice is a quota problem and not a flake.

Retry.Comment: Only what fails before a job exists. The request is built once by the step above, job name included, so a retry submits the same name -- and SageMaker refuses a duplicate with ResourceInUse. That is not a second attempt at anything: it replaces the real failure with a name clash, which is how an int8 crash was reported as ResourceInUseException. A job that was created and then failed is a cycle to look at, not to run again.

ScoreQuantizedRequest.Comment: `ScoringRequest` again, for the artifact that actually ships. One job and not a Map: exactly one seed is deployed, so exactly one model is quantized and there is one thing for the edge gate to be about. The seed is the lowest one `Score` produced, matching `evaluation.entrypoint.deployed_seed`. `instance_type` is deliberately not passed -- int8 is a CPU format, and the input an execution may set is the GPU type training and scoring share, so honouring it here would put the quantized graph on a runtime that falls back to float and measure a model the device will never run.

ScoreQuantized.Comment: The second pass over `eval`, with the int8 graph the fleet would run. Its detections land beside the fp32 ones under `precision=int8/` rather than over them, and `Evaluate` reads both to say what quantization cost. Measured here rather than on a device because neither of the edge gate's thresholds needs one, and because this is where a failure is still cheap: a quantization loss found in the cloud is a training-side change, and the same loss found after a rollout is a rollout. `.sync` owns the wait for `ScoreSeed`'s reasons, and a restart is safe for the same one.

Retry.Comment: `ScoreSeed`'s retrier, for the same reason: the job name is minted once with the request, so retrying a created job can only collide with itself.

EvaluateRequest.Comment: `ScoringRequest`'s arrangement for the job that reads ground truth: the request is built by the same function a CLI calls, so this file is a second caller of one definition rather than a second definition written in a language with no tests. One job and not a Map, because a paired delta is a mean over same-seed differences and a comparison cannot be divided across jobs -- so the whole seed list goes in one payload, taken from what `Score` assigned rather than from the execution input, and a seed that failed to score is a seed nothing tries to evaluate. `instance_type` is deliberately absent: the one an execution may set is the GPU type training and scoring share, and this job is numpy over cached arrays.

Evaluate.Comment: The job that matches this cycle's detections against the eval cohort's ground truth, caches the per-image match arrays, runs the paired bootstrap and writes the gate report. It is the one principal in the account admitted to `labels/cohort=eval/` -- scoring deliberately holds no label grant, so this is where the two halves of the plane meet. `.sync` owns the wait for `ScoreSeed`'s reasons, and a restart is safe for the same one: the job reads frozen inputs and overwrites its own outputs. A failed gate is a completed job -- the verdict is the product, and it is in the report for `Register` to read -- so a failure here is a job that could not reach a verdict at all, and it ends the cycle rather than being run again.

Retry.Comment: `ScoreSeed`'s retrier, for the same reason: the job name is minted once with the request, so retrying a created job can only collide with itself.

Register.Comment: Writes the cycle's model manifest and builds the request that records its verdict. It reaches no verdict of its own -- `Evaluate` wrote one at `conventions.gate_report_key` and this reads it -- and it refuses outright if the manifest contradicts the run registration, because that is a broken comparison rather than a rejected model. The three values it assigns are used by three different states, so they are variables rather than output: a state that had to reach into a request to find the group it creates would be a second spelling of that name. Retries are runtime faults only, for `Prepare`'s reason: ControlError is a refusal and is refused identically on a second attempt.

OpenTheRegistryGroup.Comment: One model package group per run, opened by the first cycle that reaches this state. The catch is deliberately blanket: every cycle after the first finds the group already there, and what SageMaker calls that failure is a validation error whose message is not a contract worth matching on. Nothing else is being swallowed in practice -- a group is a name rather than a resource with state, so the only other way this fails is a missing grant, and `RegisterTheVersion` cannot succeed without the same grant and reports it one state later. Opening it here rather than at run registration keeps every SageMaker call in this file, where the execution history records it.

RegisterTheVersion.Comment: The verdict as the registry records it, with ModelApprovalStatus set from the gates and the manifest attached as metadata. A rejected challenger is registered too, and that is the point: the rejection log is a feature (design section 5), and a registry holding only the approvals cannot show one. Built by the step above and created here for the reason the three job requests are -- the control function holds no SageMaker grant, so the function that builds a registration cannot make one.

Passed.Comment: The short-circuit, and it is narrower than it sounds. A failed gate leaves the champion in place and the labels stay bought, so a rejected cycle carries on through the fleet round trip to selection rather than ending -- there is no state in which a gate verdict costs the run its purchase. What it skips is the pointer flip: the champion that stays is the model that then scores this cycle's pool sample.

Promote.Comment: The champion pointer flip, and the state that makes the next cycle a comparison rather than another baseline. One conditional update on the item the cycle was claimed from, so the pointer arrives back at ClaimCycle with the cycle number. Only reached when the gates passed -- the registry already recorded the verdict either way, and promotion is what a rejected challenger is denied. The condition only ever moves forward: a version sorts lexicographically by its padded cycle within one run, so a cycle re-run against an older model is refused here rather than silently regressing the champion every later comparison is paired against. Deployment is the state after this one rather than part of it, because a rejected cycle deploys too -- the champion, carrying this cycle's sample.

Deploy.Comment: Publishes this cycle's component version over whatever model is now champion: the challenger on a cycle that promoted, the standing champion on one that did not. `$passed ? $registered : $champion` is that choice, and it is made here rather than by two states because the work either way is identical. The component version is numbered by THIS cycle and not by the cycle that trained the model -- the recipe names this cycle's replay manifest, and a component version is immutable once published, so a champion redeployed three cycles running needs three of them. Publishing is separate from deploying because only a deployment can carry a task token.

FleetScore.Comment: The cycle's pass over the unlabeled pool, which happens on the device and not in this account's compute. The token goes out as a configuration value of the deployment, the device scores `POOL_SAMPLE` frames with the int8 artifact it is running, writes the detections to S3 and calls SendTaskSuccess; this state waits in between. That wait is the cost the design accepted for a ranking produced by the model actually driving. Two hours and no retry: the timeout is the only thing between a device that cannot report and an execution waiting forever, and a retry would re-deploy onto the same hardware that just failed to answer. A device that fails loudly calls SendTaskFailure instead and the execution stops in seconds rather than in hours.

Canary.Comment: The fourth gate, and the one that could not be asked until now because it needs an artifact that has reached a device. It is a state rather than a command run afterwards for one reason only: the execution is already waiting on that device for the ranking it is about to buy from, so folding the verdict in costs nothing it was not already paying. Two decisions come out of one verdict -- `passed` says whether the rollout stands, `ranks` says whether the detections may be bought from -- and the rollback of a failed rollout happens inside the step, so a device is never left running an artifact the cycle has already judged.

Ranked.Comment: The one branch that can end a cycle having bought nothing, and it is not a gate verdict. A canary that failed on throughput still ranks: the model ran correctly and slowly, the rollout is already rolled back, and slow detections are still detections. A canary that failed on the digest or on a short pass does not, because a ranking computed from unidentified bytes is not a ranking and buying a thousand labels off it spends real budget on a fiction. That is a fault to stop for rather than a cycle to continue past, so the run ends here with the verdict's own reason.

PassNotTrusted.Comment: The device produced detections the cycle may not spend against. Nothing is bought, the rollout has already been rolled back by the canary step, and the run stops for someone to look at the device -- which is the correct response to bytes that do not hash to what the gates were reported over.

Select.Comment: Ranks this cycle's sample by mean per-object uncertainty over the detections the device wrote, and files the ranking with the batch flagged on it. One seed rather than every seed the cycle scored, unlike `EvaluateRequest`: an uncertainty score is a statement about what one detector found in one frame, so a mean over seeds would rank the pool by a model that does not exist. It is `$seeds_scored[0]`, the lowest seed and the one `Register` calls deployed -- so the model that spends the budget is the model that ships. `cycle` travels beside the version because the two can name different cycles: a rejected cycle ranks with the champion, whose version was minted earlier, and the ranking belongs to the cycle doing the buying. No job here: the pass happened on the device, and what is left is a mean per image and a sort. `replace` is carried for `Prepare`'s reason, and it is the more consequential use of that flag -- the file this writes is what the oracle charges against.

Purchase.Comment: The oracle: gate the batch against the partition, charge the ledger under an idempotency key, then read the labels and file them under this run and cycle. A different function from every other Lambda step, and the only place in the cycle that is -- this one reads `raw/labels/`, which the control function is denied outright, so the two identities are two functions over one deployment package. The batch is not in this payload: the oracle reads it out of the ranking `Select` wrote, so a retry names the same images, hashes to the same digest and replays rather than buying a second batch. `pool_remaining` is what the loop below branches on, and it now comes from what the oracle left rather than from the stub's 0 -- which is what turns a machine that stopped after one cycle into one that runs the run. Retries are runtime faults only: OracleError is a refusal and is refused identically on a second attempt, and an exhausted budget arrives under its own name.

MoreCycles.Comment: Both halves of the diagram's condition. The cap is checked again in ClaimCycle, and deliberately: this decides whether to go round, that decides whether going round is permitted, and only one of them is a lock.

Done.Comment: The run has spent its cycles or its pool. Not a failure: a run that finishes its cap is a run that finished.
